newsitem.title: UK: TENNIS-WIMBLEDON WILL REMAIN ROOF-FREE, ORGANISERS SAY.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-WIMBLEDON WILL REMAIN ROOF-FREE, ORGANISERS SAY.

text.p: Wimbledon's courts will remain open to the elements despite the rain which has played havoc with this year's championships, officials said on Thursday.

Play was washed out completely on Thursday, leaving the organisers more than 120 matches behind schedule and looking at the prospect of playing on Sunday's rest day or extending the tournament into a third week.
But putting a retractable roof over the All England Club's grasscourts was not the answer, said tournament referee Alan Mills.
"Covering a natural surface is more difficult than covering a surface like the Australian Open's," said Mills.
"I don't think the court itself would actually survive too many days with the roof closed."
The Australian Open in Melbourne has a roof that can be closed over Centre Court in case of bad weather. But the tournament is played on an artificial surface, Rebound Ace.
Fairness was also an issue, said order of play committee chairman Tim Phillips.
"What about the players who don't play on a covered court?" asked Phillips who defended the decision not to put a roof on the new Court One which has been in use for the first time this year.

"If you were to have that covered and you didn't have Centre Court covered where do you stand there? We believe that Centre Court is the home of Wimbledon. It is the one with the tradition. It's the biggest and finest court."
Phillips said he was sorry for the fans who waited stoically in the rain on Thursday and went home without seeing a ball hit. On Wednesday, only two matches were completed.
"I would love to put a giant umbrella over the championships but we haven't found the practical solution that answers all the issues."
Phillips said there were financial and structural issues to consider as well as tradition.

"This is an outdoor tournament, it's a grasscourt tournament," he said. "It is so easy to say: 'Dead simple, they built one in Australia, why didn't they do it here?' and all that. I can assure you a huge amount of thinking went into it, with some very capable people indeed."
